messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David is a 53-year-old married bus driver who came to treatment months after being sexually assaulted by a man he had picked up late at the end of a shift. He described the attack in a flat, strained voice, but the details were sharply preserved. He had been exhausted after a long day on his route and had agreed, against his better judgment, to let the passenger remain on board while he finished paperwork in a quiet terminal area. The man moved behind him in the narrow space near the driver’s seat, and what David remembers most is the sound before he fully understood what was happening: the hiss of the bus doors, the rattle of the loose partition, the man’s breathing close to his ear. He felt trapped by the confined driver’s area and overwhelmed by terror and humiliation as the assault unfolded in the seat where he had always felt in control.

In the weeks afterward, those same kinds of sounds began to pull the memory back with punishing force. The hydraulic sigh of the doors, a sudden mechanical clatter, even passengers shifting and talking behind him while he drove could make the event return as if it were happening again. He said the memory did not come back as something distant or narrative; it played “like a film,” complete and immediate, and with it came the same terror he had felt during the assault. On days when he was very tired, especially toward the end of a route, he was even more vulnerable to being thrown back into it. Fatigue seemed to weaken whatever distance he could usually keep, and then the replay would come with full intensity.

As those episodes accumulated, David had come to believe that what happened had revealed something final and unforgivable about people. He was certain that people could not be trusted, and the work he had once taken pride in now felt like daily exposure to that truth. Having strangers board his bus no longer felt routine; each rider behind him was a reminder that anyone might cross a line without warning. He spoke too of having lost faith more broadly—not only in other people, but in the basic idea that life was ordered or decent. When the sounds on the bus or the press of other people in the vehicle set him on edge, what frightened him was not just the possibility of remembering, but the conviction that the world had already shown him what it really was.

The memories themselves deepened those beliefs. Each time the assault replayed in his mind, David was flooded not only with terror but with intense shame about his body. He could not remember the event without also feeling disgraced by what had been done to him physically, and that shame hardened into the sense that something about him had been spoiled. He found himself returning again and again to the thought that he should have seen it coming, should have protected himself, should never have been vulnerable in that seat. Remembering the attack did not soften it through repetition; it seemed to confirm his mistrust and his loss of faith, as though every replay was proof that he had learned the right lesson from it.

Those beliefs, in turn, made the world feel crowded with triggers. Because he no longer trusted people, driving with passengers became charged from the moment someone stepped on board and moved behind the yellow line. Because he felt ashamed of what had happened to his body, being tired scared him in a different way too: exhaustion meant feeling less defended, less solid, closer to the helplessness he despised in himself. Even ordinary bus noises took on a special menace because he was already braced for danger and violation. By the time he heard a sharp metallic sound or sensed movement behind him, his mind was primed to connect it with the assault.

That anticipation fed back into the way the memories returned. On routes with heavier passenger loads, David would monitor every sound behind him, and the vigilance itself seemed to make the film begin. Once a fragment appeared—the hiss of the door, the feeling of someone standing too close—it became hard to stop the rest from unspooling. At home he was more withdrawn with his wife, embarrassed by how often he checked the locks and how little comfort he could take from her reassurance. He kept driving because the family needed the income, but he had started dreading late shifts and feeling trapped in his own driver’s seat.

What finally brought him to seek help was a recent shift when, after several nights of poor sleep, a passenger’s movement behind him and the sound of the door closing sent him into such a vivid replay that he had to pull over until he could steady himself. He was frightened by how quickly terror and shame could still take over, and by how certain he had become that no place with other people in it was safe. More than anything, David wanted to know whether he could drive, remember, and live in his own body without feeling ambushed by the same scene over and over again.
